grid/dims: How many numbers does a linear classifier learn? Say each input has four features, so D is four, and there are three classes, so C is three.
grid/rows: W holds one row per class, and each row holds one weight per feature. Three rows of four make twelve weights.
grid/bias: Then each class has one bias: three more.
grid/total: Fifteen parameters in all. In general, it is C times D, plus C.
grid/shape: As shapes: W is C by D, three by four, and b is a vector of C numbers.
grows/class: Add a class, and W gains a whole row, plus one more bias.
grows/side: Feed it bigger images, and every row grows longer. Twice the width and twice the height is four times the pixels, so four times the weights.
grows/data: One thing never enters the count: the number of training images. Ten or a million, W keeps the same shape.
layers/two: A two-layer network is two of these in a row. Four inputs go to five hidden units, H, and those go to the three classes.
layers/l1: The first layer has D times H weights, one per line, plus H biases: twenty plus five, twenty five.
layers/l2: The second has H times C weights, plus C biases: fifteen plus three, eighteen.
layers/sum: Add the layers: forty three. Every layer is inputs times outputs, plus one bias per output.
example/ask: Your turn. A linear classifier for see-far ten takes thirty two by thirty two color images and scores ten classes. How many parameters does it learn?
example/D: Each pixel holds three numbers, red, green and blue, so one image flattens to thirty two times thirty two times three: D is three thousand and seventy two.
example/W: W has ten rows of three thousand and seventy two weights: thirty thousand, seven hundred and twenty.
example/total: Plus ten biases makes thirty thousand, seven hundred and thirty parameters.
